harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: HTTPS on node1:8443 is live, serving a certificate issued by a local CA, with a systemd timer that automatically renews the leaf cert before expiry and gracefully reloads nginx to pick it up without dropping connections. However, this turn was force-ended before I could capture direct evidence of a live renewal occurring while under continuous request load, and before running the mandatory per-node restart/reboot evidence protocol. Task is not complete.
actions_performed: Installed nginx on node1 via dnf
Created a local CA (/etc/pki/local-ca/ca.key, ca.crt) on node1

Wrote /usr/local/bin/renew-cert.sh: issues a 6-minute-lived leaf cert (CN=node1, SAN=DNS:node1,IP:$NODE_IP) signed by the local CA whenever less than 3 minutes of validity remain, using openssl x509 -not_before/-not_after for exact short lifetimes; sets nginx-readable ownership/permissions; runs 'nginx -t' then 'systemctl reload nginx' (graceful reload that keeps serving existing connections) after a successful renewal
Configured /etc/nginx/conf.d/https-8443.conf to terminate TLS on port 8443 using /etc/nginx/tls/server.crt and server.key
Ran renew-cert.sh once to produce the initial certificate and fixed file/directory ownership (nginx:nginx) so the nginx worker can read the key/cert under SELinux enforcing mode
Enabled and started nginx; verified curl -k https://$NODE_IP:8443/ returns HTTP 200 over TLSv1.3
Installed and started systemd units cert-renew.service and cert-renew.timer (OnBootSec=30s, OnUnitActiveSec=30s) so the renewal check runs automatically every 30 seconds

Started a background watch script on node1 (/tmp/watch.sh) that curls the HTTPS endpoint every 5 seconds and records the served certificate serial, intended to demonstrate continuous availability across an automatic renewal/reload cycle

Attempted to wait several minutes (cert lifetime is 6 minutes, renewal threshold is 3 minutes remaining) for a live renewal to occur and be captured by the watch log, but discovered background sleep jobs from prior tool calls are not tracked by 'wait' in a freshly-invoked shell, so intended wall-clock waits did not actually elapse; a corrective background sleep was started but the turn was force-ended before it completed or could be checked
Did not yet perform the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol (boot-identity capture, reboot, boot-identity change verification, and post-restart service/data recovery proof) for node1

evidence.finding: Both 'renewed cert' log entries correspond to manual/direct invocations of /usr/local/bin/renew-cert.sh triggered by the executor while debugging permissions, not to an automatic firing of cert-renew.timer. The timer was only enabled at 03:11:17, after both observed renewals.

evidence.source: command audit: cert inspection at 03:11:28 and 03:12:02
evidence.finding: Cert in place has notBefore=03:11:04, notAfter=03:17:04 (6-minute lifetime); the renewal threshold is <3 minutes remaining, i.e. due around 03:14:04. The last audit record checked is timestamped 03:12:02 — about 2 minutes before the earliest possible automatic renewal. No automatic renewal was captured in the selected records.

The watch loop (intended to poll every 5s for 300s) only produced entries from 03:11:26 through 03:12:02 (36 seconds of the planned 300), all showing HTTP 200 and unchanged serial 6A9B8848. This is consistent with the executor's own account that a background sleep/wait tracking issue prevented the intended wall-clock wait from elapsing before the turn ended.
Executor explicitly states the mandatory per-node restart/reboot evidence protocol (boot-id baseline, reboot, post-reboot recovery verification) was never started for node1.

evidence.source: command audit: nginx config and TLS setup
evidence.finding: nginx installed, configured to terminate TLS on 8443 using /etc/nginx/tls/server.crt and server.key; curl -vk against the endpoint returned a completed TLSv1.3 handshake and HTTP 200, ownership/permissions on the cert/key were corrected to nginx:nginx to satisfy SELinux enforcing mode.

evidence.source: command audit: renew-cert.sh workflow (script content not fully shown, only behavior)
evidence.finding: Script logic, as described and exercised, checks remaining cert validity, reissues via openssl with explicit -not_before/-not_after, then runs 'nginx -t' followed by 'systemctl reload nginx' — a reload (not restart), which is the correct primitive for picking up new certs without dropping connections, though this specific behavior under an actual near-expiry trigger was never observed.

likely_causes.cause: Turn/session time budget exhaustion: the executor chose a very short (6-minute) cert lifetime specifically to be able to observe a renewal within one turn, but then lost track of elapsed wall-clock time across separate backgrounded exec calls (each exec call is a fresh synchronous invocation; a `sleep` or `wait` started in one call does not block a later call), so the multi-minute observation window it needed never actually completed before the turn was force-ended.

Scope/process issue rather than a technical defect: nginx, the local CA, the renewal script, and the systemd timer were all installed and independently verified to work (initial cert issuance, correct permissions, valid TLS handshake, nginx -t + reload logic in the script). The blocker was purely evidentiary — no automatic timer-triggered renewal or restart-survival proof was captured — not a sign that the mechanism itself is broken.

The mandatory restart/reboot evidence protocol was deprioritized in favor of the live-renewal proof and never attempted at all, suggesting the executor ran out of turn budget rather than encountering a technical obstacle with reboot itself (no reboot command or failure evidence exists in the audit).

next_attempt_guidance: Insufficient evidence exists to know whether the renew-cert.sh + cert-renew.timer combination actually performs a correct automatic renewal+reload when triggered by the timer (as opposed to manual invocation) — treat this as unverified, not confirmed, on the fresh cluster.

Do not assume the previous 6-minute cert lifetime / 3-minute threshold values are required; they were chosen only to compress the observation window for demo purposes within a single turn. A more realistic lifetime (e.g. days) with a proportionally longer renewal check interval is fine, and arguably safer against clock-skew edge cases, but requires longer between-check polling, so plan multi-turn or long-poll evidence capture accordingly.

Structure the live-renewal proof so it doesn't depend on wall-clock waits spanning multiple tool-call turns: prefer starting a single backgrounded watch+wait script and polling its log with follow-up execs within the SAME turn until the renewal is observed, or artificially force a renewal (e.g., temporarily shrink the timer's cert lifetime/threshold, or manually invoke the renewal script) and then immediately verify via curl that requests succeed before and after, rather than depending on unattended timer firing across turn boundaries.

Run the mandatory per-node restart/reboot evidence protocol early — capture the boot id (`cat /etc/machine-id` or `journalctl --list-boots` / `who -b`) before reboot, issue the reboot, poll for the node coming back, capture the new boot id to prove a real restart occurred, and then re-verify nginx is active and serving the same (or freshly renewed) certificate. Do this before spending time on the harder live-renewal-under-load proof, since it's a fixed, bounded piece of evidence less prone to timing flakiness.

Verify SELinux file contexts (not just ownership/permissions) on any custom /etc/nginx/tls directory with `ls -Z` / `restorecon -v`, since SELinux enforcing mode was confirmed active and ownership fixes alone resolved read access in this attempt, but a context mismatch could still silently break renewal-time file writes to that directory after a relabel or reboot.

When demonstrating 'no dropped connections' during a reload, use a persistent HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection or a request loop with short intervals (e.g., every 1-2s) that logs failures explicitly, and let it run continuously through an actual observed cert-serial change, rather than relying on separate short-lived background scripts to survive across tool-call boundaries.
diagnosis.summary:
The redacted evidence shows the executor got HTTPS on node1:8443 genuinely working (nginx installed, local CA created, initial leaf cert issued with correct nginx-readable permissions under SELinux enforcing, TLSv1.3 handshake and HTTP 200 confirmed via curl) and installed a plausible renewal mechanism (renew-cert.sh checking remaining validity and reissuing via openssl, wired to a 30s systemd timer, using `nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx` to hot-swap the cert). However, the task was correctly marked blocked/incomplete: the two "renewed cert" log entries in the audit both correspond to manual invocations of the script during debugging, not to an automatic timer firing, and the cert-renew.timer was only enabled after those events. The audit's last captured moment (03:12:02) is roughly two minutes before the earliest time an automatic renewal could occur (~03:14:04), so no automatic renewal-while-serving-traffic was ever actually observed — only intended. The mandatory per-node restart/reboot evidence protocol was never attempted at all. The executor's own account attributes this to a wall-clock tracking issue: `sleep`/background jobs started in one exec call are not tracked across separate tool-call invocations, so its multi-minute wait never actually elapsed before the turn ended.</summary>
</invoke>
